full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the Dacca High Court, setting aside in a Second Appeal a concurrent judgment of the Courts below and decreeing the suit brought by the respondents against the appellants for recovery of khas possession of the land in suit on declaration of their title thereto. 

 2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the land in suit comprises a plot of land being C. S Plot No.310 measuring '80 acre, which was recorded, along with CS. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre, as Koljote of one Mainuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of Defendants No.2 to 9, in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh P.S. Tejgaon, under the Jote of one Mani Mohan Dutta, which was recorded in Khatian No.82 of the mouza under the superior interest of one Haladhar Dey Sarkar. The father's name of Mainuddin was wrongly mentioned to be Ainuddin in Khatian No.83 in place of his correct name of Amir. The jote of Mani Mohan Dutta was put to auction in execution of a decree for arrears of rent obtained by Haladhar Dey Sarker and purchased by the decree-holder on 6-7-38. The sale was confirmed on 11-8-38 and delivery of possession of the auction purchased property was taken through Court on 23-1-39. The decree-holder auction purchaser having possessed the land for sometime settled the land of C S Plot No.311, on which the homestead was situated, with Mainuddin, son of Amir, at an annual rent of Rs. 1/6/-annas on the basis of a Kabuliyat executed on 27-3-39 and registered on 1-4-39. The other plot, namely C S. Plot No.310, remained in the khas possession of the auction-purchaser till 15-1-41, when the same was settled with the predecessor of plaintiffs No.1 to 18, and plaintiff No.19 off behalf of himself and on behalf of plaintiff No.20, on the basis of a registered Kabuliyat of the said date. Taking advantage of the wrong recording of the father's name of Mainuddin in the record-of-right defendant No.10 who happened to be an Advocate of the Dacca High Court, along with his relative defendant No.11, created some Kabalas in collusion with the heirs of Mainuddin to grab a portion of the land which has become valuable in the meantime. A dispute having arisen as to the possession of the land, defendant No.3, initiated a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in which possession having been found by the Magistrate, who was trying proceeding, in favour of the defendants, possession has been taken by the defendants from the receiver who had been appointed by the said Magistrate in the said proceeding. 

 4. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit on holding on a consideration of the evidence on record and facts and circumstances of the case, that the plaintiffs had no right title and interest in the disputed land. In course of coming to the said decision it was held that the interest of Mainuddin was an occupancy raiyati right, which was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and that even if it was not a protected interest but was merely an encumbrance, the auction purchaser could not get khas possession of the land comprised in the tenancy of Mainuddin without annulling the said incumbrance. Although the defence case that the name of Mainuddin's father was Ainuddin was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge and the father's name, as given in the Kabuliyat, Ext.3 was found to be corrects the said Kabuliyat was disbelieved as not a genuine transaction. The learned Subordinate Judge also could not place any reliance upon the Dakhalias, Ext.4 series, produced in support of the plaintiff's claim of settlement, and negatived the plea of such settlement. On the question of possession, the learned Subordinate Judge was of the opinion that although the direct evidence of barga settlement of the suit land as set up by the defence, was not satisfactory but in the facts and circumstances of the case he was not in a position to reject the defence case on this count and on an analysis of the oral evidence, adduced by both the parties, came to the finding that the plaintiffs bargadar ploughed the land for 6/7 years after the death of Mainuddin and that the sons of Mainuddin began to possess the suit land one and a half years or so after the independence of the country.
